catalog_quote: Syriem is a tonal language in which every syllable carries one of the three underlying tones. In isolation, three tones have been established: rising (low to high rise), falling (high to low fall) and low tone (fairly level but downslide before a pause). The three tones are marked over the vowel, e.g. [ǎ]=rising tone, [â]=falling tone and [à]=low tone. The occurrences of each of the three contrastive tones are provided below. ... Low tone occurs in both open and closed syllables. ... Rising tone occurs both in open and closed syllable. ... Falling tone can occur with both open and closed syllables. [p. 92] ... Syriem words are largely monosyllabic. There is one-to-one correspondence between the syllable and the morpheme boundary, especially for function morphemes. new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule is given. The only prosodic statement is that Syriem is a tone language with three contrastive lexical tones (rising, falling, low) borne by every syllable; words are largely monosyllabic, with bisyllabic stems consisting of an (unstressed-looking, low-toned) prefix plus a root. The paper never uses the words 'stress' or 'accent'.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: in closed syllables with rising tone the coda is restricted to p, t, k, m, n, ŋ, l, r, y (p. 92); long vowels of open syllables shorten when compounded (p. 93).
new_statements.domain_note: Tones are described for syllables in isolation (citation forms); no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Devi 2015/2016 call the language Syriem (a.k.a. Fyriem); Deb & Debbarma 2012 call it Saihriem and describe it as 'one of the dialects of Hmar' (hmar1241), while Glottolog syri1242 treats it as a separate West/Old Kuki language 'closely related to Aimol' (aimo1244) and Haokip 2018/2019 record intelligibility claims with Hmar. Devi's data come from the same five Cachar villages (Balisor/Kuki Punji, Noksa/Nengpur, Bagbahar, Syriem Kho, Nagathol) that Wikipedia and Deb & Debbarma list for syri1242, so the quoted source is the language of record; note Devi describes it as a mixed Kuki-Chin koine (Aimol, Thadou clans, Kholang, Rangkhol, Tollai speakers).
